hazards.haul-no-belay: You hauled on the main line with no belay. A single-line haul with a person on it is one jammed pulley or one cut sheath from a drop back into the space with the patient still attached.
hazards.no-isolation: You started the rescue with the line into the chamber still live. Whatever filled that space is still being fed into it, and it will fill again behind the entrant and the fan.
hazards.rush-in-unprotected: You went in after the patient without air or a line. More than half of the people who die in confined spaces are the would-be rescuers; the atmosphere that put the worker down is still there, and now there are two patients and nobody at the hole.
hazards.vent-into-space: You pointed the blower so it pulled from beside the exhaust. Ventilating with the discharge of an engine or the plume you just pushed out is how a space gets worse while the meter says the fan is running.

interrupts.alert: The meter on the tended line is alarming. Oxygen at the bottom of the chamber is falling while you rig.
interrupts.cue: Nobody goes in on that reading. Read the space again.
interrupts.missNote: You finished rigging and sent an entrant into a space whose oxygen was still falling. The reason the meter is lowered on a line is that the atmosphere in a chamber is not a fact you establish once — it is a thing you watch, and nobody was watching it.
interrupts.why: A space that was inside the band twenty minutes ago is not inside it now. The entry decision is made on the current worst reading, and the meter on the line exists so that reading is never more than a few seconds old.
interrupts.wrongNote: Read the meter. Nothing else in this rescue is worth doing until you know what the space is doing right now.

interrupts.alert: The attendant has left the opening to help on the rope. There is nobody tending the line or counting who is in the space.
interrupts.cue: Get somebody back on the hole.
interrupts.missNote: You hauled with nobody tending. The line fouled on the lip and the entrant was hanging with no one at the opening to see it, which is how a rescue becomes two rescues.
interrupts.why: The attendant is not spare labour. They are the only person whose job is the entrant, the only one watching the meter, and the only one who knows how many people are in that space.
interrupts.wrongNote: The hole is unattended. That is the problem, and it is the only problem, until somebody is back on it.

lateNotes.entrant-descend: The entrant goes in after the space is isolated, ventilated, monitored and the system is rigged and belayed.
lateNotes.gas-meter: Monitoring means top, middle and bottom, and it comes after the space is isolated and the fan has run.
lateNotes.haul-handle: The haul starts once the patient is packaged and the entrant calls for the lift.

name: Confined Rescue

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the permit board: what the space is, what is in it, how far down the patient is.
steps.prompt: Read the permit board: what the space is, what is in it, how far down the patient is.
steps.title: Size up the space
steps.why: Under NFPA 1006, the first decision on any confined-space call is whether this is a viable rescue or already a recovery, and that decision has to happen before a rope comes off the truck, not after someone is already committed to the hole. The permit and what is visible of the space are what a rescue technician has to work from, since nobody down there can tell them anything.

steps.cue: Physically hold back the coworker who is climbing in after their partner.
steps.holdBreakNote: You let go before the coworker stopped moving toward the hole. An untrained entry into an unassessed permit space is how a one-patient call becomes a two-patient call, and it happens in the few seconds a hold is released early.
steps.prompt: Physically hold back the coworker who is climbing in after their partner.
steps.title: Hold the crew at the hole
steps.why: More than half of confined-space fatalities are the would-be rescuers, per OSHA's own accident data behind 29 CFR 1910.146(k), and the instinct to go straight in after a downed coworker is exactly what produces that number. The job of the first rescue technician on scene is to physically hold the untrained entry back until there is actually a protected way in.

steps.cue: Close the feed valve, lock and tag it, then set the blank flange.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Valve, then lock, then blank — each step makes the last one permanent.
steps.prompt: Close the feed valve, lock and tag it, then set the blank flange.
steps.title: Isolate the space
steps.why: A closed valve is still a valve somebody else can open from a panel that has no idea a rescue is underway below it. The lock stops the hand that would turn it and the blank flange stops the line even if the valve itself fails, and both are needed together because the entrant will be under that feed line for the whole length of the rescue.

steps.cue: Turn the blower to point its intake into clean air, upwind, with the duct running to the bottom of the space.
steps.prompt: Turn the blower to point its intake into clean air, upwind, with the duct running to the bottom of the space.
steps.title: Aim and start the ventilation
steps.why: Mechanical ventilation moves air at the bottom of the shaft where the heavy gas actually sits, and per 1910.146 it has to draw from air that is genuinely clean or it is just moving the same bad atmosphere in a circle. Which way the intake is turned to face is most of whether the fan helps the entry at all or does nothing.

steps.cue: Lower the meter through the space and commit when the readings are inside the entry band.

gauge.label: O₂ / LEL
gauge.missNote: Outside the entry band — keep ventilating and read the space again before anyone goes in.

steps.prompt: Lower the meter through the space and commit when the readings are inside the entry band.
steps.title: Monitor top, middle and bottom
steps.why: Gases stratify by weight, so an oxygen reading taken at the top of a shaft says nothing about what is sitting at the bottom where the patient actually is. The meter goes down in stages under NFPA 1670, and per 1910.146 the entry decision is made on the worst reading anywhere in the space, never the first or the most convenient one.

steps.cue: Set the tripod over the opening with the legs chained, reeve the main line and mechanical advantage, then the belay on its own anchor.

itemNames.belay-line: belay line on a separate anchor

steps.outOfOrderNote: Tripod, then main, then belay — the frame is stable before anything is loaded, and the belay is never an afterthought.
steps.prompt: Set the tripod over the opening with the legs chained, reeve the main line and mechanical advantage, then the belay on its own anchor.
steps.title: Rig the system
steps.why: ANSI Z359 fall-arrest and rescue-system practice calls for two lines on two independent anchors, tripod first with its legs chained so the frame cannot spread under load, because the whole rigged system has to survive losing any single part of it — a failed carabiner, a cut sheath — while an entrant or a patient is still hanging from it.

steps.cue: Entrant on supplied air with an escape bottle, attendant at the opening with the log, comms tested.
steps.prompt: Entrant on supplied air with an escape bottle, attendant at the opening with the log, comms tested.
steps.title: Prepare the entrant
steps.why: Under 29 CFR 1910.146(k), the attendant never leaves the opening and never enters the space themselves, no matter how urgent things look inside — their entire job is the atmosphere log, the tended line, and knowing exactly how many people are in that space at any moment, because that count is what a second rescuer needs the instant something goes wrong.

steps.cue: Lower on the main line at a steady, controlled rate with the belay tracking.
steps.holdBreakNote: Lowering rate out of band — the belay cannot track that. Bring it back and hold.
steps.prompt: Lower on the main line at a steady, controlled rate with the belay tracking.
steps.title: Lower the entrant
steps.why: A controlled, steady lower keeps the entrant off the walls and any fixed ladder in the shaft, and keeps the belay tender able to track the rate rather than reacting to a rope that is suddenly running free. Speed on the way down buys nothing — the entrant still has to size up the patient before doing anything — and it costs the one thing this rig is built to give them, which is control.

steps.cue: Airway first with supplied air, then the rescue harness, then clip to the main line.

itemNames.patient-airway: airway and air on the patient
itemNames.patient-clip: patient clipped to the main line

steps.outOfOrderNote: Airway, then harness, then the clip — the patient is breathing before they are lifted.
steps.prompt: Airway first with supplied air, then the rescue harness, then clip to the main line.
steps.title: Package the patient
steps.why: Air before movement, always: the patient has been breathing whatever atmosphere put them down, and moving them before they are on supplied air just extends that exposure. The rescue harness distributes the lift across the body instead of one point, and the clip to the main line goes on last so nothing on the patient is under tension while the harness is still being fitted.

steps.cue: Haul on the mechanical advantage at a steady rate while the belay is minded.
steps.holdBreakNote: Haul rate out of band — steady it before the patient hits the edge.
steps.prompt: Haul on the mechanical advantage at a steady rate while the belay is minded.
steps.title: Haul the patient out
steps.why: A steady haul on the mechanical advantage lets the attendant actually watch the patient clear the opening instead of reacting to a rope that lurches, and it keeps the belay tender able to hold tension without guessing. Jerking a haul line with a person on the end of it is what breaks an edge roller, catches a limb on the lip, or dislocates a shoulder that is already injured.

steps.cue: Patient to EMS with what they were breathing, the atmosphere log to the incident commander, and the space tagged closed.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Patient, then the log, then the space — care first, evidence second, scene last.
steps.prompt: Patient to EMS with what they were breathing, the atmosphere log to the incident commander, and the space tagged closed.
steps.title: Hand over and secure
steps.why: The hospital treats the patient on what the atmosphere meter actually recorded, not on a verbal description of what the space looked like from the surface. The atmosphere log travels with the patient to EMS, and the space itself stays tagged closed until the employer's post-incident investigation under 1910.146 is complete, because it is now the scene of a permit-space rescue.

tagline: Below-grade rescue: refuse the unprotected entry, isolate and ventilate, monitor top to bottom, tripod and mechanical advantage rigged, air-supplied entrant on a tended line, patient packaged, controlled haul, atmosphere log handed over
